planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; common bamboo is one of the most widely distributed bamboos in the tropics and subtropics but is frost-tender and only reliably hardy in the warmest parts of zone 9 and up.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with room for a large, dense clump, since this tropical timber bamboo forms tall, thick culms and does not run aggressively the way many temperate bamboos do. Common bamboo is among the most widely cultivated bamboos in the tropics worldwide, valued for fast-growing, sturdy culms used in construction, furniture, and crafts, with the striking yellow-and-green-striped cultivar 'Vittata' grown as an ornamental specimen far more often than the plain green species. It is frost-tender and drops leaves or dies back in a hard freeze, so it suits only the mildest parts of the Gulf Coast reliably, needing winter protection or a sheltered microclimate farther north within its zone range. Water deeply during establishment and dry spells, and thin out old, congested culms at the base each year to keep the clump vigorous and allow new shoots room to emerge.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; pygmy bamboo spreads by running rhizomes and is best contained with a root barrier or an isolated bed edged by pavement or a mowed strip.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, containing the planting with a buried root barrier, mowed edge, or hardscape boundary since this bamboo spreads by running rhizomes into a dense, low mat. Pygmy bamboo is among the smallest bamboos grown, staying under a foot and a half tall with fine, narrow leaves that give it a grassy, groundcover texture entirely unlike the towering canes most people picture when they hear 'bamboo,' making it useful for erosion control on slopes, edging, or filling in as a low, evergreen groundcover in difficult sites. It tolerates mowing once or twice a year like a lawn if a very low, uniform carpet is wanted, and it spreads fastest in moist, fertile soil, so lean, drier sites naturally slow its spread. Once established it needs little care beyond an occasional mowing or trimming to remove tattered winter foliage before spring growth resumes.

common_name: Species Lenten Rose (Wild Hellebore, Parent of the Garden Hybrids)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall, or plant container divisions in fall or early spring, in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade; seed needs a period of warm-then-cold stratification and often takes a full year to germinate.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline, well-drained soil under deciduous trees or on the north side of structures where it gets bright shade year-round. Helleborus orientalis is the wild Balkan and Turkish species behind the vast majority of modern garden hellebore strains sold as Helleborus x hybridus, and true species plants are still available through specialist growers for gardeners who want the straightforward, unimproved wild form — nodding, cup-shaped flowers in shades of green, cream, and dusky purple-pink held above leathery, evergreen, palmately divided foliage from late winter into early spring. It is exceptionally long-lived and low-maintenance once established, tolerating deer, drought once the canopy leafs out, and root competition from nearby trees far better than most shade perennials, though it resents transplanting and is best left undisturbed for years at a stretch. Cut back tattered old winter foliage in late winter just as new flower stalks emerge, and all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where pets or children graze on greenery.
